items.text: Updating the document encoder BERTd during training is costly as it requires the document index to be periodically updated as REALM does during pre-training [20].
items.why: Explains a training optimization that leaves document embeddings frozen.
items.plain: Updating the document encoder during training is expensive because it requires periodically updating the document index.

items.text: We do not ﬁnd this step necessary for strong performance, and keep the document encoder (and index) ﬁxed, only ﬁne-tuning the query encoder BERTq and the BART generator.
items.why: States an ablation choice that keeps document embeddings fixed.
items.plain: We keep the document encoder and index fixed, training only the query encoder and the generator.

items.text: For more efﬁcient decoding, we can make a further approximation that pθ(y|x, zi) ≈0 where y was not generated during beam search from x, zi.
items.why: Describes an approximation made in Fast Decoding.
items.plain: For faster decoding, we assume the probability of generating a text given a document is zero if that text was not created during beam search for that document.

items.text: MSMARCO has some questions that cannot be answered in a way that matches the reference answer without access to the gold passages, such as “What is the weather in Volcano, CA?” so performance will be lower without using gold passages.
items.why: Notes a dataset limitation affecting maximum achievable performance.
items.plain: Some questions in MS-MARCO cannot be answered to match the reference without reading the provided gold passages, which lowers performance when those passages are not used.

items.text: We also note that some MSMARCO questions cannot be answered using Wikipedia alone.
items.why: States a domain coverage limit in the non-parametric index.
items.plain: Some MS-MARCO questions cannot be answered using Wikipedia alone.

items.text: Crucially, unlike most other approaches to FEVER, we do not use supervision on retrieved evidence.
items.why: Highlights the lack of retrieval supervision in the FEVER experiment.
items.plain: Unlike most other approaches to FEVER, we do not train our model using labels for which evidence passages should be retrieved.

items.text: It is worth noting that RAG’s retriever is initialized using DPR’s retriever, which uses retrieval supervision on Natural Questions and TriviaQA.
items.why: Clarifies that the retriever initialized with DPR relies on prior retrieval supervision.
items.plain: The retriever starts with weights from Dense Passage Retriever, which was trained using retrieval supervision on Natural Questions and TriviaQA.

items.text: Furthermore, RAG can generate correct answers even when the correct answer is not in any retrieved document, achieving 11.8% accuracy in such cases for NQ, where an extractive model would score 0%.
items.why: Claims generation success even when target text is missing from retrieved context.
items.plain: Our model answers Natural Questions correctly 11.8% of the time when the correct answer is missing from all retrieved documents, whereas extractive models score 0%.

items.text: To assess the effectiveness of the retrieval mechanism, we run ablations where we freeze the retriever during training.
items.why: Presents an ablation where the retriever module is kept frozen.
items.plain: To evaluate the retrieval training, we test a version where the retriever parameters are frozen during task training.

items.text: We compare RAG’s dense retriever to a word overlap-based BM25 retriever [53].
items.why: Introduces a non-neural baseline comparison using BM25.
items.plain: We compare our dense neural retriever to a traditional word-matching BM25 retriever.

items.text: For FEVER, BM25 performs best, perhaps since FEVER claims are heavily entity-centric and thus well-suited for word overlap-based retrieval.
items.why: Acknowledges that a simple BM25 baseline outperforms the neural retriever on FEVER.
items.plain: BM25 retrieval achieves better results than our dense retriever on the FEVER task.

items.text: Accuracy with mismatched indices is low (12% with the 2018 index and 2016 leaders, 4% with the 2016 index and 2018 leaders).
items.why: Shows severe performance drops when the index is mismatched with facts.
items.plain: When using a 2018 index for 2016 world leaders, accuracy falls to 12%, and using a 2016 index for 2018 leaders drops accuracy to 4%.

items.text: Effect of Retrieving more documents Models are trained with either 5 or 10 retrieved latent documents, and we do not observe signiﬁcant differences in performance between them.
items.why: Notes no substantial performance change between training with 5 versus 10 documents.
items.plain: Training with 5 or 10 retrieved documents shows no significant difference in overall performance.

items.text: Figure 3 (left) shows that retrieving more documents at test time monotonically improves Open-domain QA results for RAG-Sequence, but performance peaks for RAG-Token at 10 retrieved documents.
items.why: Shows performance ceiling when retrieving more documents at test time.
items.plain: Retrieving more documents at test time consistently improves question answering for RAG-Sequence, but RAG-Token performance stops improving after 10 documents.

items.text: We use greedy decoding for QA as we did not ﬁnd beam search improved results.
items.why: Explains a decoding choice where beam search provided no gain.
items.plain: We used greedy decoding for question answering because beam search did not improve the results.

items.text: We use a beam size of four, and use the Fast Decoding approach for RAG-Sequence models, as Thorough Decoding did not improve performance.
items.why: States an approach failure where Thorough Decoding failed to help RAG-Sequence.
items.plain: We used a beam size of four and fast decoding for RAG-Sequence models, because thorough decoding did not improve performance.

items.text: Two annotators did not perform well on these examples and their annotations were removed from the results.
items.why: Notes human annotator exclusion that could affect evaluation validity.
items.plain: We removed the annotations of two annotators because they did not perform well on test examples.

items.text: CuratedTrec preprocessing The answers for CuratedTrec are given in the form of regular expressions, which has been suggested as a reason why it is unsuitable for answer-generation models [20].
items.why: Identifies dataset format limitations that make it unsuitable for answer generation.
items.plain: CuratedTrec answers are formatted as regular expressions, which makes the dataset unsuitable for answer-generation models.

items.text: We ﬁnd that our performance is much higher using the ofﬁcial Wiki test set, rather than the more conventional open-domain test set, which we attribute to the ofﬁcial Wiki test set questions being simpler to answer from Wikipedia.
items.why: Explains a performance discrepancy driven by test set question difficulty differences.
items.plain: Our performance was much higher on the official Wikipedia test set than on the standard open-domain test set, likely because the official Wikipedia questions are easier to answer using Wikipedia.

items.text: As FEVER uses a different Wikipedia dump to us, directly tackling this task is not straightforward.
items.why: Notes a data mismatch limitation preventing direct evaluation on a sub-task.
items.plain: Because FEVER uses a different Wikipedia version than we do, tackling the sentence extraction task directly is not straightforward.

items.text: We did not ﬁnd that these improved performance, so in the interests of simplicity, we omit them.
items.why: Reports negative results for the tested null document mechanisms.
items.plain: Adding null document mechanisms did not improve performance, so we omitted them to keep the model simple.

items.text: The T5 model with the closest number of parameters to our models is T5-large (770M parameters), which achieves a score of 28.9 EM on Natural Questions [52], substantially below the 44.5 that RAG-Sequence achieves, indicating that hybrid parametric/nonparametric models require far fewer trainable parameters for strong open-domain QA performance.
items.why: Claims parametric-hybrid models outperform pure parametric models with fewer parameters.
items.plain: T5-large has 770 million parameters and gets 28.9 Exact Match on Natural Questions, whereas RAG-Sequence reaches 44.5, showing that hybrid models need far fewer trainable parameters to perform well in open-domain question answering.

items.text: In preliminary experiments, we observed that for some tasks such as story generation [11], the retrieval component would “collapse” and learn to retrieve the same documents regardless of the input.
items.why: Identifies a failure mode where the retrieval component collapses.
items.plain: In preliminary experiments on tasks like story generation, the retriever collapsed and fetched the same documents regardless of the input.

items.text: In these cases, once retrieval had collapsed, the generator would learn to ignore the documents, and the RAG model would perform equivalently to BART.
items.why: Explains the impact of retrieval collapse on generator performance.
items.plain: When retrieval collapsed, the generator learned to ignore the retrieved documents and performed no better than standard BART.

items.text: The collapse could be due to a less-explicit requirement for factual knowledge in some tasks, or the longer target sequences, which could result in less informative gradients for the retriever.
items.why: Speculates on the underlying causes of retrieval failure in certain tasks.
items.plain: Retrieval collapse might happen because some tasks require less explicit factual knowledge, or because longer target text produces less informative training signals for the retriever.
